'''''Galium boreale''''' or '''northern bedstraw'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17}}</ref> is a species of perennial [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Rubiaceae]]. It is widespread over the temperate and subarctic regions of Europe, Asia and North America including most of Canada and the northern United States.<ref>[http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=85836 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]</ref><ref>[http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Galium%20boreale.png Biota of North America Program]</ref><ref>[http://luirig.altervista.org/flora/taxa/index1.php?scientific-name=galium+boreale Altervista Flora Italiana]</ref>

==Description==
''G. boreale'' is a [[perennial plant]] that dies back to the ground every winter.<ref name="NatureGate">{{cite web |title=Northern Bedstraw, ''Galium boreale'' - Flowers - NatureGate |url=http://www.luontoportti.com/suomi/en/kukkakasvit/northern-bedstraw |website=www.luontoportti.com |publisher=NatureGate Promotions Finland |accessdate=2 June 2019}}</ref><ref name="Budd">{{cite book |last1=Budd |first1=A.C |last2=Looman |first2=J. |last3=Best |first3=K.F. |title=Budd's Flora of the Canadian prairie provinces. |date=1987 |publisher=Research Branch, Agriculture Canada |location=Ottawa |isbn=0-660-10233-1 |edition=Rev. and enl. |url=https://archive.org/details/buddsfloraofcana0000budd |accessdate=2 June 2019 |url-access=registration }}</ref> Established plants spread by [[rhizome]]s, creating colonies of new plants around the original one.<ref name="NatureGate"/><ref name="Budd"/><ref name="ERA"/>

The squarish unbranched stems may grow between {{convert|20|cm|in}} and {{convert|50|cm|in}} tall.<ref name="NatureGate"/><ref name="Budd"/> The leaves are attached directly to the stem in groups of four; spaced evenly like the spokes of a wheel.<ref name="NatureGate"/><ref name="Budd"/><ref name="ERA"/> Leaves are longer than they are wide and have three prominent veins.<ref name="NatureGate"/><ref name="Budd"/><ref name="ERA">{{cite journal |last1=Smreciu |first1=A. |last2=Gould |first2=K. |last3=Wood |first3=S. |title=''Galium boreale'': northern bedstraw, sweet scented bedstraw, fragrant bedstraw |url=https://era.library.ualberta.ca/items/cc697db1-b7c0-488e-ab4b-27fe74574c2b |website=ERA |publisher=University of Alberta |accessdate=2 June 2019 |language=en |date=3 December 2013|doi=10.7939/R3JH3D60S }}</ref>

The small white flowers grow in a fairly showy [[panicle]]s from the top of the stem.<ref name="NatureGate"/><ref name="Budd"/><ref name="ERA"/> Each individual flower has 4 pointed segments that fold back from a fused tube enclosing the [[stamen]]s and [[pistil]].<ref name="NatureGate"/><ref name="Budd"/> The lightly perfumed flowers have no [[sepal|calyx]].<ref name="NatureGate"/><ref name="Budd"/> Seeds are formed in pairs in dark fruits that may be covered in short hairs.<ref name="NatureGate"/><ref name="Budd"/><ref name="ERA"/> The Latin specific epithet ''boreale'' means northern.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Galium boreale - Plant Finder|url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=286665|access-date=2022-02-22|website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}}</ref>

==Habitat and distribution==
''Galium boreale'' is found in sunny areas with dry to moist soil in forests, shrubs or [[grassland]].<ref name="NatureGate"/><ref name="Budd"/> It is native to the sub arctic and temperate zones of the Northern Hemisphere.<ref name="POTWO"/><ref name="ERA"/> It is listed as endangered in the states of Maryland and Massachusetts.<ref>{{cite web |title=Plants Profile for ''Galium boreale'' (northern bedstraw) |url=http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=GABO2 |website=plants.usda.gov |access-date=2 June 2019}}</ref>

==Ecology==
''Galium boreale'' is confirmed as a food plant for the larvae of ''[[Deilephila elpenor]]'', ''[[Deilephila porcellus|D. porcellus]]'', ''[[Epirrhoe galiata]]'', ''[[Eupithecia subumbrata]]'' and ''[[Gandaritis pyraliata]]''.<ref>{{cite web |last=Savela |first=Markku |url=https://www.nic.funet.fi/pub/sci/bio/life/plants/magnoliophyta/magnoliophytina/magnoliopsida/rubiaceae/galium/#boreale |title=''Galium boreale'' L. |website=Lepidoptera and Some Other Life Forms |accessdate=30 June 2019}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
The species ''Galium boreale'' was first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753 based on the European population.<ref name="SP1753">{{cite web |last1=Linnaeus|first1=Carl |authorlink=Carl Linnaeus|title=Species Plantarum IV-V |url=https://www.gutenberg.org/files/27049/27049-h/27049-h.htm |website=www.gutenberg.org |accessdate=2 June 2019}}</ref><ref name="POTWO">{{cite web |title=''Galium boreale'' L. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:749626-1 |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |accessdate=2 June 2019}}</ref> 
{{Quote
|text=Galium foliis quaternis lanceolatis trinerviis glabris, caule erecto, seminibus hispidis.
|author=Carl Linnaeus
|title="Galium boreale"
|source=''Species Plantarum'' (1753)
}} 
In 1818, ''Galium septentrionale'' Roem. & Schult. was described by [[Johann Jacob Roemer]] and [[Josef August Schultes]] based on the North American population.<ref name="POTWO"/><ref name="scoggan">{{cite book |last1=Scoggan |first1=H.J. |title=Flora of Manitoba |date=1957 |publisher=National Museum of Canada |location=Ottawa}}</ref> ''G. septentrionale'' was determined to be a synonym of ''G. boreale'' in 2003.<ref name="POTWO"/>

The genus ''[[Galium]]'' is a member of the family [[Rubiaceae]].<ref name="POTWO"/>

==Uses==
''Galium boreale'' is edible, with a sweet smell and taste, and can be eaten as a wild salad green. Varieties such as ''Galium boreale'' which do not contain the small hooks on the stem are not as palatable as the hooked varieties of ''Galium'', like ''[[Galium aparine]]'', but are important plants to remember for survival purposes.<ref>Edible and Medicinal Plants of the West, Gregory L. Tilford, {{ISBN|0-87842-359-1}}</ref> ''Galium boreale'' is known as "bedstraw" because it is used as fragrant stuffing for mattresses.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Galium boreale (northern bedstraw): Go Botany|url=https://gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org/species/galium/boreale/|access-date=2021-11-02|website=gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org}}</ref> There is also chemical evidence for its roots use in red textile dyes during the "Viking age" (year 800 to 1066).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Viking Age Dyestuffs |url=https://www.cs.vassar.edu/~capriest/vikdyes.html |access-date=2022-05-05 |website=www.cs.vassar.edu}}</ref>
